entities.summary:
Neubrandenburg, founded in 1248 by John I, Margrave of Brandenburg, stands as a prime example of a planned medieval town in the German region of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Its strategic location on the northern shore of the Tollensesee, an expansive lake, made it a vital outpost for the expanding Margraviate of Brandenburg, intended to secure territories against the Duchy of Pomerania and to control emerging trade routes. The city's original layout, a rectangular grid enclosed by a remarkably preserved medieval wall system, reflects a deliberate act of urban planning, distinguishing it as a significant medieval foundation in Northern Europe and a testament to the systematic territorial expansion of the Brandenburg margraves.

The city's development was characterized by rapid growth, facilitated by its role as a regional administrative and commercial center. Its most striking architectural features, the four ornate Brick Gothic gatehouses—Stargarder Tor, Friedländer Tor, Treptower Tor, and Neues Tor—were constructed between the 13th and 15th centuries, forming integral parts of the 2.3-kilometer medieval wall. These structures, along with the Wiekhäuser (small defensive houses built into the wall), represent some of the most complete and best-preserved medieval fortifications in Northern Europe. Economically, Neubrandenburg benefited from its position on trade routes, though it never achieved the full economic stature of the major Hanseatic cities.
